title: Multi-Account Strategy: Organizations, Control Tower & SCPs

scenes.narration: This chapter opens the Professional half of the course — from here on, this material maps to the AWS certified solutions architect Professional exam, sometimes written S A P dash C zero two, rather than the associate exam you may already have passed. It opens with one sentence that carries most of its exam weight: a Service Control Policy — say the letters, S C P — can only ever restrict permissions, never grant them, and it's evaluated alongside your identity policies, I A M for short, never instead of them. Organizations, organizational units, consolidated billing, and Control Tower's landing zones all exist mainly to give that one restriction mechanism somewhere sensible to attach. This is the start of Design Solutions for Organizational Complexity, twenty six percent of the professional exam — the second largest of its four domains.

facts.label: The one rule
facts.value: An SCP can only restrict permissions, never grant them — evaluated alongside IAM, never instead of it

facts.label: Where this sits
facts.value: SAP-C02 · Organizational Complexity, 26% of the exam

scenes.narration: Two wrong instincts show up constantly here, and the exam loves baiting both in the same question. The first: seeing many teams, many environments, many cost centers, and reaching for what already works at small scale — one account, groups per team, tags per environment. That's the right call for three engineers; it's the trap answer for an enterprise. The second, sneakier instinct: reading an allow statement inside a policy attached to an organizational unit and assuming every principal underneath can now use that service freely, even ones with no identity policy granting it at all. That's a completely natural but completely wrong reading. The policy is a filter, not a grant — it draws the outer ceiling of what could ever be allowed, never the floor.

props.heading: "One account, careful IAM" and "a policy Allow means allowed"
bullets: Treating an enterprise like a three-person startup: one account, IAM groups per team, tags per environment.
Reading a policy's Allow statement for a service and assuming every principal underneath can now use it freely.
Missing that the default FullAWSAccess policy is a no-op ceiling, not something that grants anything.

scenes.narration: Walk through exactly why an allow statement in one of these policies doesn't mean allowed. AWS evaluates every applicable policy at once. If your identity policy allows the action and the org-wide policy also allows it, you're through. If your identity policy allows it but the org-wide policy denies it — or simply leaves it off an allow-list — you're blocked, and that restriction wins. If your identity policy never granted the action in the first place, an org-wide allow does nothing; there's nothing to grant. And if your identity policy explicitly denies it, no org-wide policy can out-allow that. Effective permission is always the intersection of the two, never the union — and the default policy AWS attaches to every root, every organizational unit, and every account is a single allow-everything statement, a deliberate no-op you carve down from there.

props.heading: Why an SCP Allow doesn't mean allowed
steps: IAM allows it, SCP allows it too → permitted
IAM allows it, SCP denies or excludes it → denied, the SCP wins
IAM never grants it, SCP allows it → still denied, nothing to grant
IAM explicitly denies it → denied, no SCP can out-allow that
Effective permission = IAM-allow ∩ SCP-allow — the intersection, never the union
Default FullAWSAccess SCP = one Allow: * statement, a no-op you carve down from

scenes.narration: Put those four outcomes side by side and the pattern becomes mechanical. Both layers agreeing to allow something is the only case where the action actually goes through. The moment the org-wide policy restricts it — denies it outright, or just leaves it off an allow-list — that restriction wins, full stop. If nothing in your identity policy ever mentioned the action, an org-wide allow is meaningless; there was never anything to grant. And an explicit deny in your identity policy is final — no broader policy can override it. Four rows, one rule: intersection, not union.

props.heading: Every combination the exam actually tests

scenes.narration: This table resolves most of the exam's guardrail questions, and the axis that matters most is preventive versus detective. An org-wide restriction reaches every principal in every account it covers, including that account's own administrators and root user — use it when an account's own admins can't be trusted to leave a guardrail alone. A permission boundary caps just one role or user inside one account, and that same account's administrators can still edit or remove it — fine when the account owner is trusted to maintain it. Control Tower's preventive guardrails are just these same org-wide restrictions, pre-written and consistently applied, so there's no custom document to author. Its detective guardrails are different in kind entirely — built on configuration-monitoring rules that observe and report after the fact, sometimes triggering remediation, but never blocking the action up front.

props.heading: SCP vs permission boundary vs Control Tower guardrail

rows.label: Service Control Policy
cells: Every principal in scope, including that account's own admins and root
An account's own admins can't override the guardrail from inside

rows.label: IAM permission boundary
cells: One IAM user or role, one account
That single principal — the account's admins can still edit or remove it
You cap one role, and the account owner is trusted to maintain it

rows.label: CT preventive guardrail
cells: An OU, implemented as an SCP
You want the SCP protection, pre-written and consistently applied

rows.label: CT detective guardrail
cells: An OU, implemented as a Config rule
Nothing in real time — observes and reports after the fact
The action can't be prevented upfront, but drift must be caught

scenes.narration: None of this works if you don't also know its edges — these are the specific facts that turn into gotcha distractors. A single policy document tops out at five thousand, one hundred twenty characters; a long list of region exemptions can hit that ceiling surprisingly fast. Organizational units nest five levels deep at most, counting the root itself, and every level you add is one more document getting intersected together. The management, or payer, account is never restricted by policies attached to it — which is exactly why serious landing-zone guidance keeps it almost empty of real workloads. Service-linked roles are deliberately exempt, so a broad restriction can't silently break AWS's own managed automation running underneath a service. And exact quotas move over time — if a scenario turns on a number you're not confident in, answer from the decision framework, not a guessed figure.

props.heading: The fine print the exam turns into gotchas
bullets: SCP document size limit: 5,120 characters — long region-exemption lists hit it fast.
OUs nest 5 levels deep at most, root included — every level intersects one more document.
The management account is never restricted by SCPs attached to it — keep it nearly empty of workloads.
Service-linked roles are exempt, so a broad deny can't silently break AWS's own automation.
Exact quotas move — answer from the framework, not a guessed number, when unsure.

scenes.narration: Three commands map to the three moves this chapter is built around. Creating the organization with the all-features flag is what actually turns the restriction mechanism on — the consolidated-billing-only mode doesn't support it. Authoring a policy with create-policy doesn't restrict anything by itself; it just produces a document and hands you back an ID. The restriction only takes effect once you separately call attach-policy and point that ID at a real target — an organizational unit, an account, or the root. Recognizing that authoring and attaching are two distinct steps, and that a scenario describing the outcome of one of these calls is asking you to predict what happens next, is an extremely common exam pattern.

props.heading: Create, author, attach — three separate steps

output: # ALL is required for SCPs — CONSOLIDATED_BILLING alone won't do

steps.cmd: aws organizations create-policy --name RegionRestriction --type SERVICE_CONTROL_POLICY --content file://region-restriction.json

output: Policy attached — the OU's accounts are now restricted
Nothing was restricted until this exact call ran

scenes.narration: You'll never be asked to write this from memory, but recognize the shape. create-org dot s h runs once and turns the calling account into the management account. create-ous dot s h builds the organizational-unit tree — security, infrastructure, workloads, and sandbox — before a single real account gets placed into it. The policies folder holds separate, single-purpose documents: one blocking an account from ever leaving the organization, one locking every action to approved regions, one protecting the central logging bucket even from that account's own administrators. And attach-policies dot s h is the step that actually turns any of those documents into a live restriction, one attach call per target.

props.kicker: THE LANDING ZONE, ORGANIZED BY INTENT
props.heading: landing-zone/
lines: │   ├── create-org.sh          # one-time — enables all features + billing
└── attach-policies.sh         # one attach-policy call per OU

scenes.narration: Take a concrete case. Meridian is a fast-growing SaaS company with sixty AWS accounts already spread across business units, no consistent guardrails between them, and forty more product teams to onboard over the next two quarters. Today, standing up a new account means a human copying an identity baseline, reattaching the standard restrictions, and manually wiring up centralized logging — roughly a day of work, with an occasional forgotten step. Run it through the framework: this is exactly the many-new-accounts, consistent-guardrails, minimal-custom-scripting scenario. The answer is Control Tower's Account Factory — every new account lands in the right organizational unit with the same preventive and detective guardrails and the same logging wiring already in place, without anyone re-typing the same setup forty times and eventually missing a step on account twenty seven.

props.heading: Scaling account creation faster than a platform team can type

scenes.narration: Try these before we reveal the answers. First: a Workloads organizational unit has a policy that's a single allow statement covering only EC2, S3, and Lambda actions — nothing else — and a developer's identity policy separately grants DynamoDB access. Can that developer actually write to DynamoDB? Second, and this is one of the single most-tested facts in the domain: an administrator signed into the management account tries an action that a policy on the organization root explicitly denies. What actually happens?

questions.prompt: A Workloads OU's SCP is a single explicit Allow statement covering only EC2, S3, and Lambda actions. A developer account under that OU has an IAM policy granting DynamoDB PutItem. Can the developer actually write to DynamoDB?
options: Yes — IAM already granted it, and the SCP doesn't mention DynamoDB at all
No — an explicit allow-list SCP replaces the default full-access ceiling, and anything not listed is outside the account's maximum permissions
Yes, but only through the console, not the CLI
No — DynamoDB is excluded from every SCP by default

questions.prompt: An administrator signed into the organization's management account attempts an action that an SCP attached to the organization root explicitly denies. What happens?
options: The action is denied — root SCPs apply to every account in the organization
The action succeeds — SCPs attached to the root or the management account never restrict the management account itself
The action succeeds only if the administrator also has AdministratorAccess
The action is queued for manual approval by a Control Tower guardrail

scenes.narration: Here's why. Once an explicit allow-list restriction is attached, it functionally replaces the default allow-everything ceiling — anything left off that list, DynamoDB included, is outside the account's maximum available permissions no matter what the identity policy grants. That's the allow-list flavor of restrict-only, never-grant. And the management-account question is the sharper one: the action succeeds. A restriction attached to the organization root, or directly to the management account, restrains every member account underneath it — but never the management account itself. That's exactly why serious landing-zone design keeps that one account running almost no workloads: it's the single place the guardrails can't reach.

answers.prompt: Can the developer write to DynamoDB under that allow-list SCP?
answers.correct: No — the allow-list SCP excludes DynamoDB entirely, regardless of what IAM grants.
answers.rationale: An explicit allow-list SCP functionally replaces the default FullAWSAccess ceiling. IAM's grant is still real, but DynamoDB PutItem simply falls outside the OU's maximum available permission set — the exam's favorite allow-list variant of 'SCPs can only restrict.'

answers.prompt: What happens when a root-level SCP denies an action the management account attempts?
answers.correct: The action succeeds — SCPs attached to the root or the management account never apply to the management account itself.
answers.rationale: This is one of the most frequently tested facts in the domain. Root and management-account SCPs restrain every member account underneath, but never the management account — exactly why landing-zone guidance insists it run almost no workloads of its own.

scenes.narration: Five things to carry forward. A restriction like this can only narrow what's possible, never widen it, and it's always evaluated alongside your identity policies — effective permission is the intersection of the two, never their union. The management account is exempt from restrictions attached to it, which is exactly why it should stay nearly empty. A single account can't build an org-wide guardrail on its own, because the same administrators who'd need restraining also control the restraint — separate accounts buy blast-radius isolation, clean billing separation, and a compliance boundary policy correctness alone can't match. Know the real numbers: a five thousand, one hundred twenty character size limit, organizational units nesting five levels deep including the root, and a default policy that's a deliberate no-op. And whenever a scenario describes standing up many new accounts at scale with consistent guardrails, Control Tower's account-vending automation is almost always the intended answer over hand-rolled scripting. Next: chapter seventeen moves from who's allowed to do what, to how all these accounts actually talk to each other — Transit Gateway, Direct Connect, and hybrid connectivity across the whole estate.

props.heading: What to remember from this chapter
takeaways: SCPs can only restrict, never grant, and are always evaluated alongside IAM — effective permission is the intersection, never the union.
The management account is exempt from SCPs attached to it — keep it nearly empty of real workloads.
A single account can't build an org-wide guardrail — separate accounts buy blast-radius isolation, billing separation, and a compliance boundary policy alone can't match.
Know the real numbers: 5,120-character SCP limit, 5-level OU nesting including root, and a default FullAWSAccess no-op.
Standing up many new accounts at scale with consistent guardrails almost always means Control Tower's Account Factory, not hand-rolled scripting.

scenes.narration: One more to work through yourself. A regional bank's Workloads organizational unit has an explicit allow-list restriction covering only EC2, S3, RDS, and Lambda actions. A newly hired administrator, working entirely inside one member account, writes an identity policy granting a role full access to K M S, the key management service. Using this chapter's framework, can that role actually use K M S — and what specifically would have to change for it to work?
